newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Spat with France puts EP's powers under spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Spat with France puts EP's powers under spotlight.

text.p: The European Parliament -- lambasted by France this week for interfering in its internal affairs -- is facing a challenge to the way it uses its existing powers just when it is seeking new ones.
France on Thursday demanded help from its European Union partners to rein in the assembly after condemning it for urging Paris to withdraw a controversial immigration bill.

The president of the parliament, Jose-Maria Gil-Robles, had earlier cancelled a meeting with French Foreign Minister Herve De Charette on Wednesday after the French minister branded the legislature "not yet a parliament worthy of the name".
The spat bodes ill for the parliament's search for new powers, which is already turning into an uphill struggle as the EU's inter-governmental review of its workings goes into its final months.
Set up as the European Community assembly in 1957, the parliament is seeking in the review to correct a power imbalance which leaves it the poor relation of national parliaments.

Directly elected for the first time in 1979, the 626-seat assembly can help negotiate the EU's budget, sack the European Commission, approve EU plans to admit new members and seal major trade deals like the customs union with Turkey.
Although it has never used its power to sack the Commission, veto a new member or block a major trade deal, it has cried wolf on several occasions.
Under the Maastricht Treaty on European Union which came into force in 1993 the parliament's powers were increased to give it joint decision-making powers in a number of areas.
But it still very often negotiates from a position of weakness, needing an absolute mahjority of 314 votes to force changes on the European Commission and member states.

All too often the parliament gets into the spotlight when it exercises its moral weight as the EU's directly elected assembly on a Thursday afternoon of plenary sessions, adopting non-binding resolutions on everything from human rights to natural disasters, often when few members are in the house.

In such a motion narrowly adopted last week the parliament urged the centre-right French government to withdraw its bill aimed at further tightening laws on illegal immigration that would allow stricter monitoring of legal third world visitors.

De Charette, extending a bitter clash with the Strasbourg-based assembly, said he would ask foreign ministers from the other 14 nations "to reflect on the European Parliament's exceeding its responsibilities".
The parliament "must fully exercise its responsibilities, but only those, and not interfere in the French process, in the legislative process. To each his job," de Charette told France Inter radio.
The dispute illustrates scepticism in France about a drive by the parliament to gain wider powers at the expense of national parliaments.

In the inter-governmental review the parliament is seeking to simplify EU making procedures to spread its joint decision- making powers to more areas, give it more power over the budget and the right to sack individual commissioners.
France and Britain have opposed extending its powers while Germany is in favour. Even so, France has widely funded the parliament and pushed to anchor it in Strasbourg rather than Brussels.
